title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
authors: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, Pieter Abbeel

pages.title: Generate by reversing a noising process

blocks.html: The problem. Generative modeling asks: after seeing many real images, produce new ones from the same distribution. GANs (in this collection) do it with an unstable adversarial game; VAEs do it with a single latent code but tend to blur. DDPM proposes a third route that is both stable to train and produces GAN-quality samples — by learning to undo a gradual corruption process.

The intuition / analogy. Imagine slowly dripping ink into a glass of water until the image dissolves into a uniform cloud — that is the easy direction, pure physics, no learning. Now imagine being able to run the film backwards: starting from the cloud and watching it re-condense into a crisp picture. DDPM trains a neural network to perform exactly that reverse step. Generation becomes: start from random noise, then take many tiny denoising steps until a clean image emerges.

items: Forward process (fixed, no learning): take a real image $x_0$ and add a little Gaussian noise. Repeat $T$ times (the paper uses $T=1000$). After enough steps the image is indistinguishable from pure $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ noise.
Reverse process (learned): start from pure noise $x_T\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and remove a little noise at a time, step by step, until you reach a clean sample $x_0$.
The surprise: the whole reverse process collapses to one simple task — at each step, a network just predicts the noise that was added — trained with a plain mean-squared-error loss.

blocks.html: We present high quality image synthesis results using diffusion probabilistic models, a class of latent variable models inspired by considerations from nonequilibrium thermodynamics.

Why it mattered. The headline result was that diffusion models could finally match GANs on image quality (CIF-10 FID of 3.17) while remaining a stable, likelihood-flavored model with no adversarial training and no mode collapse. This paper is the technical foundation of the 2022–2024 image-generation explosion: Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2, Imagen, Midjourney, and video models like Sora and Veo are all descendants.

pages.title: Where diffusion sits among generative models

blocks.html: The intuition. Before judging the math, it helps to see why this design is attractive. Each of the prior families had a defining weakness: GANs train via a saddle-point game that is unstable and prone to mode collapse (generating only a few kinds of output); VAEs optimize a clean likelihood bound but the single-step Gaussian decoder produces soft, averaged samples. Diffusion keeps the VAE's principled, likelihood-based objective and reaches GAN-level sharpness, by replacing one hard generation step with hundreds of easy ones.

The key reframing. A diffusion model is a latent-variable model $p_\theta(x_0)=\int p_\theta(x_{0:T})\,dx_{1:T}$, where the latents $x_1,\dots,x_T$ are noisier and noisier versions of the data, all the same dimensionality as $x_0$. In VAE language: it is a very deep hierarchical VAE whose encoder is fixed (the forward noising chain, with no learnable parameters) rather than learned. All the learning goes into the decoder — the reverse chain.

Why split generation into many steps. Asking a network to jump from pure noise to a photorealistic face in one shot is hard (that is the GAN/VAE decoder's job, and it is where they struggle). Asking it to make an image slightly less noisy is easy, and a near-Gaussian step is provably enough when each noise increment $\beta_t$ is tiny. Stacking many easy steps yields a powerful generator from simple parts — the central bet of the paper.

Context. The diffusion idea traces to Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015) and connects to score-based generative models (Song & Ermon). DDPM's contribution was making it work at high quality, largely through the simplified noise-prediction objective and the right network/parameterization choices covered on the following pages.

pages.title: The forward (noising) process and its closed form

blocks.html: The goal. Define a fixed, parameter-free way to turn any image into noise, gradually, so that we have a well-defined process for the network to learn to reverse.
The single forward step. The forward process $q$ is a Markov chain that adds a little Gaussian noise at each step:

Reading every symbol. $x_{t-1}$ is the image at the previous step; $x_t$ is the slightly noisier next one. $\beta_t\in(0,1)$ is the variance schedule — how much noise to inject at step $t$ — set small and increasing linearly from $\beta_1=10^{-4}$ to $\beta_T=0.02$ over $T=1000$ steps. The factor $\sqrt{1-\beta_t}$ shrinks the signal a touch so the variance stays bounded; $\beta_t I$ is the added isotropic noise. Crucially there is nothing to learn here.

The closed-form shortcut (the trick that makes training cheap). You do not have to simulate the chain step by step. Because composing Gaussians gives a Gaussian, you can jump to any timestep $t$ directly from the clean image $x_0$:

Reading it. $\alpha_t = 1-\beta_t$ is the fraction of signal kept at step $t$; $\bar\alpha_t$ is the cumulative product — the fraction of the original signal surviving all the way to step $t$. As $t\to T$, $\bar\alpha_t\to 0$, so $x_T$ is essentially pure $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ noise. The practical payoff: to make a training example at timestep $t$ you sample one noise vector $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and set $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ — a single operation, no chain to unroll.

pages.title: The reverse (denoising) process and the variational bound

blocks.html: The goal. The forward process destroys information; we need to learn to put it back. That learned reverse chain is the actual generative model.
The single reverse step. The reverse process is also a Markov chain, but Gaussian with learned parameters, run from $x_T$ back to $x_0$:

Reading it. Given the current noisy image $x_t$ and the timestep $t$, a neural network outputs the mean $\mu_\theta(x_t,t)$ and covariance $\Sigma_\theta(x_t,t)$ of where the slightly-cleaner $x_{t-1}$ should be. The chain starts at $p(x_T)=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. The key justification: when each forward step's $\beta_t$ is tiny, the true reverse conditional is itself approximately Gaussian — so a Gaussian parameterization is not a crude hack but a good approximation.

How we train it: the variational bound. As in a VAE, we cannot maximize $\log p_\theta(x_0)$ directly, so we maximize a lower bound (minimize its negative). The bound decomposes over timesteps into a sum of KL divergences:

Reading it. $L_T$ has no learnable parameters (it just checks that $x_T$ is noise) and is essentially zero. Each $L_{t-1}$ compares the network's reverse step $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ against the true posterior $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ — which is available in closed form (another Gaussian) precisely because we condition on the original $x_0$. $L_0$ is the final reconstruction term. The whole objective is a sum of Gaussian-vs-Gaussian KLs, each of which is just a squared difference of means — there is no adversary and no high-variance sampling, which is why training is stable.

pages.title: Predict the noise: from KL to L_simple

blocks.html: The problem. The per-step KL term $L_{t-1}$ asks the network's mean $\mu_\theta(x_t,t)$ to match the true posterior mean. That works, but DDPM's central practical insight is a reparameterization that turns this into something far simpler and better-conditioned: instead of predicting the cleaned image, predict the noise.

The reparameterization. Recall $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$. If the network can guess the noise $\epsilon$ that was mixed in, it implicitly knows $x_0$, and the reverse-step mean follows in closed form:

Reading it. $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ is the network's prediction of the injected noise. The formula simply subtracts a scaled version of that predicted noise from the current image and renormalizes — so the network never has to output a full image, only a noise estimate of the same shape.

The simplified loss. Substituting this into the KL terms and then dropping the time-dependent weighting (the paper found the unweighted version trains better and acts as a useful emphasis on harder, noisier steps) yields the famous objective:

Reading it as a recipe. (1) Sample a clean image $x_0$ from the dataset. (2) Sample a timestep $t$ uniformly from $\{1,\dots,T\}$. (3) Sample noise $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. (4) Build the noisy image $x_t$ in one shot. (5) Ask the network to predict $\epsilon$, and minimize the mean-squared error. That is the entire training loop (the paper's Algorithm 1) — strikingly close to a denoising autoencoder, and nothing like a GAN's delicate balancing act.

The network. $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ is a U-Net (an encoder-decoder with skip connections, plus self-attention at lower resolutions) conditioned on the timestep $t$ via a Transformer-style sinusoidal positional embedding. A single set of weights handles every timestep — $t$ is just an extra input — so the model size does not grow with $T$.
The goal. Turn the trained noise-predictor into an image generator (the paper's Algorithm 2).
The procedure. Start from pure noise $x_T\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. Then for $t=T, T-1, \dots, 1$, take one ancestral-sampling step:

items: Draw the next, cleaner image $x_{t-1} = \mu_\theta(x_t,t) + \sigma_t z$, with fresh $z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ for $t>1$ and $z=0$ at the final step. DDPM fixes $\sigma_t^2=\beta_t$ (or the posterior variance $\tilde\beta_t$) rather than learning it.

blocks.html: The cost / the catch. After $T$ such steps you have a sample $x_0$. The downside is speed: $T=1000$ steps means 1000 sequential network forward passes per image — orders of magnitude slower than a GAN's single pass. This is the one place diffusion clearly loses, and it motivated a wave of follow-up acceleration work: DDIM (deterministic, non-Markovian sampling in 20–50 steps), distillation, and modern fast solvers (DPM-Solver, Karras schedulers).

pages.title: Image quality, FID, and the design ablations

blocks.html: The headline numbers. On CIFAR-10 unconditional generation, DDPM reaches an FID of 3.17 and an Inception Score of 9.46 — at publication, the best FID among likelihood-based models and competitive with strong GANs (FID is the Fréchet Inception Distance; lower is better, as it measures how far generated-image statistics sit from real ones).

High resolution. On LSUN (church, bedroom) and CelebA-HQ at $256\times256$, DDPM produces samples that are visually comparable to GANs — sharp and globally coherent — but without the mode-collapse and training-instability pathologies that plague adversarial training. The model simply covers the data distribution because its likelihood-based objective rewards doing so.

The crucial ablation. The paper compares the full variational bound $L$ against the simplified, unweighted $L_{\text{simple}}$, and finds $L_{\text{simple}}$ gives better sample quality despite being a worse log-likelihood. The down-weighting of small-$t$ (low-noise) terms that $L_{\text{simple}}$ implies turns out to focus the network on the perceptually important high-noise steps. They also confirm that predicting $\epsilon$ beats predicting $\mu$ directly or predicting $x_0$ — the noise parameterization is what makes the method shine.

Progressive generation. Because sampling reveals the image coarse-to-fine, DDPM can show a striking 'progressive decoding' visualization: large-scale structure (pose, layout) is decided in the early, high-noise steps and fine detail (texture, edges) is filled in near the end — mirroring the autoregressive idea but over noise scales rather than pixels.

Why it changed the field. DDPM was the moment diffusion models became competitive with GANs on quality, and they arrived with a bundle of structural advantages that the GAN (earlier in this collection) never had:

items: Stable training: a simple MSE regression objective, no minimax game, no balancing two networks — runs of training reliably converge.
Full distribution coverage: no mode collapse, because the likelihood-based bound penalizes ignoring parts of the data.
Easy conditioning: text, class labels, or other images can steer generation, later via classifier and classifier-free guidance.
The cost: slow, multi-step sampling — the main weakness, since addressed by faster samplers and distillation.

blocks.html: Direct descendants. Improved DDPM (cosine noise schedule, learned variances), classifier-free guidance, score-based SDE formulations, latent diffusion (operating in a compressed VAE latent space — the basis of Stable Diffusion), consistency models, and rectified flow all build directly on this work.

The lineage in this collection. DDPM is best understood sitting between the two papers around it: it inherits the variational lower bound and latent-variable framing from the VAE (it is a deep hierarchical VAE with a fixed encoder), and it dethrones the GAN on the very metric — sample quality — that GANs had owned since 2015. It is the technical foundation of the 2022–2024 generative-image explosion: DALL·E 2, Imagen, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, and video models like Sora and Veo.
